title: C1 quiz: toolchains and the build pipeline

items.q: In gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c11 hello.c -o hello, what does -o hello do?
choices: Names the output executable hello (instead of the default a.out)
Turns on optimization level hello
Opens hello.c for reading
Runs the program after compiling it
items.why: -o sets the output file name. Optimization is -O (capital letter, a number after it), and gcc never runs your program: the ./hello after && does that.

choices: It makes the program run faster
It turns every warning into an error, so code with a likely bug can't build
It hides warnings so the output is cleaner
It is required to link printf
items.why: A warning means 'legal, but probably not what you meant'. With -Werror the build stops until you understand and fix it, like refusing to run a line while a fault light is on. Many professional firmware builds use it.

items.q: You compile a file and get: undefined reference to 'pritnf'. Which stage of the pipeline reported it?
choices: The preprocessor
The compiler
The linker
The bootloader
items.why: 'undefined reference' is the linker's message: your object file calls a function named pritnf and no library provides it. (The compiler only warned about an implicit declaration; with -Werror, that warning stops the build even earlier.)

choices: Links the standard I/O library into the program at run time
Pastes the text of the stdio.h header in, so the compiler knows the declarations of printf and friends
Downloads the stdio library from the internet
Starts the serial port
items.why: #include is a preprocessor directive: pure text pasting, before compiling. The header holds declarations; the actual printf code is in the C library, which the linker connects later.

choices: AB (on one line, then a newline)
A and B on two separate lines
Nothing, because there is no newline after A
A compile error: printf needs a newline
items.why: printf prints exactly what you give it. Unlike Python's print, it never adds a newline, so A and B land on the same line, and the \n after B ends it.

items.q: What does main() returning 0 mean on the desktop?
choices: The program printed zero characters
Success: the shell sees exit status 0 (check it with echo $?)
The program will restart
An error occurred
items.why: The return value of main is the exit status. 0 means success and anything else means failure. Scripts, make, check.sh, and CI pipelines all read it, the way a PLC reads a drive's 'done OK' bit.

items.q: An Arduino sketch has setup() and loop() but no main(). Where is main()?
choices: There is none: the ATmega328P runs setup() directly from reset
In the Arduino core library: it calls init(), then setup() once, then loop() forever
The IDE runs loop() repeatedly from Windows over USB
In the bootloader
items.why: The core's main.cpp does init(); setup(); for (;;) { loop(); }. The linker joins your sketch to it. The bootloader only loads new programs; it is not part of your program's run.

items.q: Inside loop() you add delay(2000). In PLC terms, what have you done?
choices: Added a timer that runs in the background while other logic continues
Stretched the scan time to more than 2 seconds: nothing else in loop() runs during the delay
Changed the baud rate
Nothing important: delay only affects the LED
items.why: delay() blocks. The CPU sits in a busy wait, so every other input check and output update in loop() waits too, like a slow rung that stretches every scan. Non-blocking millis() timing (C14) fixes this.

items.q: Your sketch calls Serial.begin(115200), but the Serial Monitor shows random garbage characters. Most likely cause?
choices: The Uno's flash is full
The Serial Monitor's baud setting does not match 115200
The LED is on pin 13
The sketch has no main()
items.why: Both ends of a UART must agree on the bit rate. If the monitor samples at 9600 while the Uno sends at 115200, it decodes the wrong bits, exactly like a scope's UART decoder set to the wrong baud.

items.q: Upload fails with 'port busy' or 'access is denied' on COM3. What should you check first?
choices: Whether another program (a second Serial Monitor, a Python script with pyserial) already has COM3 open
Whether the sketch has a syntax error
Whether -Wall is enabled
Whether the LED is burnt out
items.why: Only one program can hold a serial port. The compile succeeded (that's a different message); the upload step (avrdude) could not open the port. Close the other user of COM3. This comes up constantly once your Python logger exists.

items.q: Which part of the Arduino upload pipeline writes your program into the Uno's flash?
choices: avr-gcc
The Serial Monitor
avrdude on the PC, talking over USB serial to the bootloader on the Uno
The preprocessor
items.why: avr-gcc builds the .hex file. avrdude sends it over USB serial to the bootloader, which writes it into flash and then jumps to your program.

interview.q: Walk me through what happens between writing a C file and having it run on a microcontroller.
rubric: Names the preprocessor stage (#include and #define are text substitution)
Explains that the compiler turns C into assembly/machine code for the specific target CPU (a cross-compiler such as avr-gcc for an AVR)
Explains linking: object files are joined with libraries (startup code, the C library, the Arduino core) and addresses are resolved
Describes getting the image onto the chip (hex/bin file, programmed through a bootloader over serial or through a hardware programmer/debugger)
Mentions that reading which stage an error came from (compile error vs undefined reference) tells you where to look

interview.q: What's the difference between a desktop C program's main() and an Arduino sketch's setup() and loop()? Why doesn't firmware main() return?
rubric: Desktop: the OS loads the program and calls main(); returning hands an exit status back to the OS
Arduino: the core supplies main(), which initializes the hardware, calls setup() once, then calls loop() in an infinite loop
Explains that bare-metal firmware has no OS to return to, so main() must never exit (it would run off into undefined behavior)
Connects it to a PLC scan cycle or super-loop: each pass reads inputs, runs logic, writes outputs
Notes that blocking calls such as delay() stretch the loop and starve everything else, so real firmware uses non-blocking timing or interrupts
